summary: SPHEREx Sky Blink is a public website that lets anyone check NASA SPHEREx infrared images for things that move or change. SPHEREx photographs the whole sky again and again, so the same patch of sky is captured on many dates. For eight fields we prepared aligned frames in six wavelength bands. Visitors play the frames like a blink comparator, then report whether a bright spot moved, changed brightness, or nothing changed, and can leave a comment. Extra tools help them judge what they see: an overlay of detector-flagged pixels so they don't report artifacts, an experimental difference view, a 2MASS reference image of the same patch of sky, and an Inspect tool that gives sky coordinates and checks SIMBAD. Because the images are prepared in advance, the site loads instantly and works even when the archive is busy. It addresses the challenge by turning many pairs of eyes into a first screen of SPHEREx data for changes, and it teaches visitors what each of SPHEREx's six bands shows.
details:
What it does: visitors pick a field, play SPHEREx frames in date order, switch between six wavelength bands, and report what they saw (a spot moved, changed brightness, or nothing changed) with an optional comment. A moderated Discussion tab lets people talk about each field. Tools: detector-flag overlay (shows pixels SPHEREx's own pipeline flagged, so artifacts aren't reported), an experimental difference view, hover coordinates, a scale bar and compass, a 2MASS reference image, and "Inspect a spot", which gives coordinates and checks SIMBAD.

How it works: a Python pipeline downloads SPHEREx cutouts from NASA/IPAC IRSA, aligns the frames onto one sky grid, applies one shared brightness stretch per band, builds difference images and flag overlays, and produces PNG files and JSON. The site is a static page (HTML, CSS, JavaScript) on Netlify. Answers and comments are stored in Supabase; comments are reviewed before they appear.

Tools: Python (astropy, astroquery, reproject, numpy, scipy, scikit-image, Pillow, s3fs), HTML/CSS/JavaScript, Supabase, Netlify, GitHub.

Creativity and factors: the pipeline is precomputed, so the page is fast and doesn't depend on the archive. We designed the layout for different screen sizes, and the checking tools reduce false reports.

Limits: the Difference view is experimental; five fields have all six bands and three have Band 2 only; coordinates are approximate.

Use of AI: we used Claude (Anthropic) via chat and the VS Code extension for code, page layout and drafts; the team chose the idea, ran and tested everything, and wrote the field descriptions. Details: docs/AI_USE.md in the repository.
